attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction on his Substack, listed under his 'High confidence' heading. It is not a quotation of anyone else.

semantics.note: An unqualified 'will' under 'High confidence' makes this a scored forecast. 'Possibly' hedges only the narrow-use exception, not the main claim. The normalised proposition keeps hype, unreliability, the exception and the 2025 horizon.

contract.note: 'Endlessly hyped' and 'far from reliable' are unmeasured, and the evaluator supplied readings: promotion across 2025 and high failure rates on broad multi-step tasks. These readings are reasonable. Results this lopsided (2.5%, 30%) would hold under any plausible reading. Narrow uses are excluded, as the speaker stated.

evidence.note: Jan 2025 promotion of agents joining the workforce by OpenAI's CEO. It shows hype early in the year. It is a company statement and says nothing about reliability.
June 2025 claim that agents now do real cognitive work. It shows promotion continuing mid-year. It is a company claim, not a test.
Independent preprint revised Sep 2025. The best agent completed only 30% of realistic workplace tasks, and long-horizon tasks were beyond reach. Simpler tasks were often solved.
Oct 2025 launch of agent tooling by OpenAI. It shows promotion in Q4 2025. Its Klarna support example is a narrow use, which the speaker excepted.
Independent multi-sector benchmark published 30 Oct 2025. The best agent automated only 2.5% of real paid projects, so agents were far from reliable on broad work late in 2025.

output.rationale: The horizon ended 2025-12-31. Agents were promoted by OpenAI in January, June and October 2025, covering the whole year including Q4. Independent tests from Sep and late Oct 2025 show general-purpose agents failing most realistic multi-step tasks (best 30%, and 2.5%). Apparent counterexamples such as customer support and coding fall under the speaker's narrow-use exception. No December test exists, but the late-October data meets the contract.
